MUQATIL:7:7-9/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:7:7-9/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:7:7-9/r3.claim: The people with light scales are disbelievers, who lose themselves by denying that the Qur'an came from God.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p165#5/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p165#5/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p165#5/r1.claim: Here yaẓlimūn means they deny God's signs; the root ẓulm has several senses discussed in al-Mushkil.

TAB-FULL:v10p73/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p73/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v10p73/r1.claim: Doing wrong to God’s signs means rejecting His proofs and indications instead of affirming their validity and being certain of their truth.

TAB-FULL:v10p73/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p73/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v10p73/r2.claim: Mujahid glosses “light scales” as light good deeds.

TAB-FULL:v10p73/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p73/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v10p73/r3.claim: The singular forms من and فأولئك are used because the sense is plural; using a singular result would also be correct and eloquent.

IBNABIHATIM:v5p1441/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1441/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1441/r1.claim: Mujahid says those whose scales are light are those whose good deeds are few or light.

IBNABIHATIM:v5p1441/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1441/r2.speaker: عبيد الله بن الغيزار
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1441/r2.claim: Ubayd Allah ibn al-Ghayzar describes the crowded Resurrection and an angel announcing that the heavy-scaled are blessed forever and the light-scaled are wretched forever.

THALABI:v4p216/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r1.claim: Weighing deeds tests faith in worldly life, marks the saved and doomed in the next, shows people their recompense, and establishes the proof against them.

THALABI:v4p216/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r2.claim: The weighing is comparable to the record that speaks with truth and sets out people’s deeds, despite God already knowing them.

THALABI:v4p216/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r3.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v4p216/r3.claim: Mujahid identifies the heavy balance-pan with a person’s good deeds.

THALABI:v4p216/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r4.claim: The phrase about wronging God’s signs means that they deny them.

THALABI:v4p216/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r5.speaker: حذيفة
THALABI:v4p216/r5.claim: Gabriel weighs people’s deeds; wrongdoers’ good deeds transfer to victims, or victims’ sins are loaded onto them, leaving them burdened like mountains.

THALABI:v4p216/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v4p216/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas describes a balance with tongue and two pans: a believer’s beautiful deeds outweigh sins and lead to Paradise, while a disbeliever’s ugly deeds are light and fall into Hell.

THALABI:v4p216/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r7.claim: Since deeds are accidents, the weighed objects are written records containing people’s deeds.

THALABI:v4p216/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r8.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
THALABI:v4p216/r8.claim: A man’s ninety-nine enormous sin-records are outweighed by a tiny card bearing the testimony that there is no deity but God and Muhammad is His messenger.

THALABI:v4p216/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r9.claim: The weighing is linked to the promise that just balances will be set up for the Day of Resurrection.

THALABI:v4p217/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p217/r1.claim: The plural mawazin may be a plural form with singular meaning, like plural terms in the cited verse and al-Aʿsha’s poetry.

THALABI:v4p217/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r2.speaker: الأعشى
THALABI:v4p217/r2.claim: Al-Aʿsha’s line uses plural ‘breasts’ and ‘forearms’ while intending one of each.

THALABI:v4p217/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p217/r3.claim: Other interpretations take the plural as the deeds being weighed, or as one great balance with a balance for each servant.

THALABI:v4p217/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p217/r4.claim: The plural can refer to the whole balance assembly: its two pans, beam, and tongue, which must come together for weighing.

THALABI:v4p217/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p217/r5.claim: A moral interpretation calls reason the balance distinguishing truth from falsehood, knowledge the balance distinguishing lawful from unlawful, and sound will the balance distinguishing felicity from misery.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r1.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r1.claim: Muqatil identifies those with light scales as disbelievers.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says a disbeliever's deeds appear in their ugliest form, weigh little, and lead him to the Fire; a believer whose good deeds are light is rescued by the testimony of God's oneness and Muhammad's messengership.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p27/r3.claim: A further report says the Prophet produces a fingertip-sized card of the believer's blessings upon him; it outweighs his deeds, and the Prophet identifies it when the believer asks who he is.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p28/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p28/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p28/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas explains losing oneself as arriving at punishment and wronging God's signs as rejecting what Muhammad brought.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:9-11/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:9-11/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:9-11/r1.claim: Those with light scales lose themselves through punishment because they denied what Muhammad brought from God.

JISHUMI:v4p2499/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r3.claim: Weighing compares two things to reveal their relative measure, then extends metaphorically to prosody and measured speech; thaqal is opposite lightness.

JISHUMI:v4p2499/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r4.speaker: أبو هاشم
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r4.claim: Abū Hāshim treats heaviness as a distinct attribute in a heavy object: a necessary downward tendency.

JISHUMI:v4p2499/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r5.speaker: أبو علي
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r5.claim: Abū ʿAlī says heaviness reduces to the parts composing the heavy object; they agree that lightness is no positive attribute but the absence of heaviness.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r1.claim: Light scales describe those who deny God’s signs.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r2.speaker: أبو بكر
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r2.claim: Abu Bakr says scales grow heavy through following truth in worldly life, even when truth weighs upon people; following falsehood makes them light.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r3.claim: One explanation takes the plural form موازين as singular in meaning, like the plural address يا أيها الرسل.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r4.claim: Another explanation assigns every servant an individual balance.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r5.claim: A third view posits one great balance with a separate balance suspended for each servant.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p215/r6.claim: The plural may also refer to the balance’s two pans and indicator, whose combined parts are needed for weighing.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r2.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r2.claim: One group takes scales and weighing as a metaphor for the meticulous justice of Judgment, using the familiar image of a balance; Abu Talib's verse illustrates this sense.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r3.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the metaphorical view is weaker: Qur'anic wording and a Prophetic report direct a person to seek the Prophet at the visible balance, weighing poses no problem, and abandoning the literal sense without cause risks denying revealed realities.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r4.speaker: مجاهد، الضحاك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r4.claim: This metaphorical view is also reported from Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and others, who understand heaviness and lightness as the abundance or scarcity of good deeds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r5.speaker: جمهور الأمة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r5.claim: The majority say the Judgment balance has a beam and two pans like worldly balances, displaying exact justice through a familiar object.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r6.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r6.claim: Hudhayfa says Gabriel is the custodian of the balances on Judgment Day.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r1.claim: The balance should be understood literally; reports say records of good and bad deeds go into its pans, where God creates heaviness or lightness.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r2.claim: Weight must occur in a body, since an accident cannot inhere in another accident; it may occur in the records or nearby bodies, and Abu al-Maali favors the records.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r3.claim: Unreliable reports about the balance's shape and length need not be repeated; Hasan's report that each person has a separate balance is rejected because the balance is one, though each person has an individual weighing.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r6.claim: God's weighing, recording deeds, and making limbs testify despite His knowledge serve to establish proof; the testimony of divine oneness must tip a person's balance.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r7.claim: The author asks how sinful believers can have a weighty balance and be judged successful yet still enter Hell.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r1.claim: A light balance means the pan of good deeds rises; they lose themselves through destruction and eternal residence in Hell.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r2.claim: Bi-mā expresses recompense, like thanking someone for what they did; mā is a verbal noun, and God's signs are proofs, commands, and prohibitions that they wrong by disbelief and denial.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r3.speaker: طائفة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r3.claim: One answer is that good deeds are weighed without tawhid first, then tawhid makes the balance heavy when sinful believers are released from Hell.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r4.claim: Knowing that a sinner will not remain forever in Hell counts as success, even if disciplinary punishment comes first.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r5.speaker: طائفة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r5.claim: One answer is that good deeds are weighed without tawhid first, then tawhid makes the balance heavy when sinful believers are released from Hell.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r6.claim: Knowing that a sinner will not remain forever in Hell counts as success, even if disciplinary punishment comes first.

TABRISI:7:8-9/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:8-9/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:7:8-9/r4.claim: Those with light scales lose themselves by incurring everlasting punishment; their loss is the destruction of their greatest capital, the self, through wrongdoing and denial of Muhammad's signs.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r1.claim: God will report to the messengers and nations what they did, knowing it and never being absent from them.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r2.claim: The record will be placed and will speak of what people used to do.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r1.claim: Yazlimun means either deny or disbelieve.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r2.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r2.claim: Mawazin means weight; Arabic uses “your scale” or “your house's scale” to mean equal to or beside it, as a poem uses mizan for a person's words.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r3.claim: Belief in the scale is well established in hadith and is the Qur'an's plain sense, though the Mu'tazila deny it because deeds are accidents.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص عن النبي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r4.claim: A hadith says a man with ninety-nine vast records receives a card bearing the two testimonies; the card outweighs all records. Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi transmit it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r5.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r5.claim: A tall, gluttonous man will weigh no more than a mosquito's wing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r6.claim: Good and bad deeds are weighed on a scale with a tongue and two pans; a believer's good deeds appear beautiful and outweigh the bad, while an unbeliever's appear ugly and are light.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r7.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r7.claim: The scale has a tongue and two pans.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r8.claim: In a report, David asks to see the scale and how anyone can fill its pans; God says a date fills them when He is pleased with His servant.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r9.speaker: حذيفة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#4/r9.claim: Gabriel operates the scale; he returns a wronged person's due from the oppressor's good deeds, or transfers the victim's sins to the oppressor if no good remains.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p171/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p171/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p171/r1.claim: Although God knows the measure of deeds, weighing them tests belief in this life, displays each person's fate, teaches what good and evil they did, establishes proof, and shows that God is just; recording deeds similarly does not imply fear of forgetting.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r1.claim: The weighing follows the questioning and accounting described earlier; the phrase can be parsed with يومئذ as an adverb and الحق as predicate, or as predicate with الحق describing a just weighing.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r2.claim: One literal view says God sets up a balance with a pointer and two pans; Ibn Abbas says the believer's deeds appear in their best form and good deeds outweigh evil, as in 21:47.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says a believer's deeds are transformed into a beautiful image for weighing, while most exegetes instead say the weighed items are the written records; a prophetic answer to what is weighed is reported as the records.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r4.claim: Ibn Salam describes a balance between jinn and humans facing the Throne, with one pan toward Paradise and one toward Hell, large enough to hold the heavens and earth, watched by Gabriel.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r5.claim: Ibn Umar reports a man whose 99 scrolls of sins, each as long as sight, are outweighed by a tiny card bearing the testimony that none is god but God and Muhammad is His messenger.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r6.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r6.claim: Hasan reports that when Aisha asked about people remembering one another at resurrection, the Prophet said they would be barefoot and unclothed and too occupied with records and weighing to remember anyone, citing 80:37.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r7.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r7.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says a huge, voracious drinker may have no weight even equal to a gnat.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r1.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك والأعمش
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r1.claim: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-A'mash, followed by many later scholars, take the balance as justice and judgment rather than a literal scale.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r2.claim: Supporters of the figurative reading say weight can mean justice because worldly fairness in taking and giving is shown by weights; Arabic also uses weight figuratively for worth and equality, as in 18:105.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r3.claim: A poem cited by the author uses ميزانه for the balance of an opponent's argument: the speaker had a measure for every disputant, meaning a reply of equal force, not a physical scale.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r4.claim: Razi insists the verse must mean only justice: deeds are transient accidents, so cannot be weighed; even if they persisted, weighing is useless because believers already know God's justice and others could suspect a staged result.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r5.speaker: أصحاب القول الأول
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r5.claim: Literal-scale proponents answer that everyone knows God is just and the scale publicly displays the result: a favorable balance increases joy, an unfavorable one increases grief and shame; some describe light or darkness, others a tilted pan.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r1.claim: Razi finds several actual balances more apparent than one, citing 21:47 and the verse's plural; separate balances may measure heart, bodily, and spoken acts.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r2.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r2.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the plural either as Arabic using a plural for one object or as referring to the things weighed, meaning deeds rather than balances; Razi says both abandon the plain plural despite no obstacle to multiple scales.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r3.claim: The heavy and light balances divide humanity into two groups: those whose good deeds exceed their bad and those whose bad exceed their good; no group has equal totals.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r4.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r4.claim: Most exegetes identify those whose balances are light as unbelievers, because being described as wronging God's signs means denying them.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r5.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r5.claim: Al-Wahidi's al-Basit reports that the Prophet's prayer-card can outweigh a believer's weak good deeds; the wider scholarly report instead gives the card bearing the testimony of faith, which al-Qadi says must be paired with its obligations to avoid encouraging sin.

BAYDAWI-FULL:7:9/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:9/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:9/r1.claim: Those whose scales are light have lost themselves by wasting their sound original disposition and committing acts that expose them to punishment; they wrong the signs by rejecting them.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#4/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#4/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#4/r1.claim: The light balances belong to unbelievers: lacking faith, they have no good works that count in the scale.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#4/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#4/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#4/r2.claim: They lose themselves by wronging God's signs; the signs are proofs, and wronging them means denying them and refusing to follow them.

QASHANI:7:8-9/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:7:8-9/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:7:8-9/r1.claim: Weighing is assessment of deeds at the lesser resurrection and is just or real; lasting good deeds weigh heavily and yield the heart's paradise of divine attributes.

QASHANI:7:8-9/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:7:8-9/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:7:8-9/r2.claim: The scale's tongue is justice, with sense and intellect as its pans; enduring rational acquisitions, virtues, good works, and sincere intentions have weight, unlike transient sensations, desires, and vices.

QASHANI:7:8-9/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:7:8-9/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:7:8-9/r3.claim: The light-weight lose themselves by trading original capacity for worldly debris and personal aims, displaying ego qualities and concealing God's qualities in denial of His signs.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r10.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r10.claim: Hasan holds that every person has a separate balance on the Day of Resurrection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r11.claim: Balances can also stand for good deeds by ellipsis: the balance-pan of a person’s weighed deeds becomes heavy or light.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r14.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r14.claim: The prepositional phrase about God’s signs attaches to wronging because the verb includes the sense of denying or rejecting, and rejection takes bi-.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r15.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r15.claim: The apparent division includes obedient and sinful believers as well as unbelievers, so unbelievers’ deeds are weighed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r16.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r16.speaker: قوم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r16.claim: Others say unbelievers receive no balance and are not judged, citing the verse that their deeds become scattered dust; on this view only believers’ deeds are weighed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r4.claim: Exegetes disagree whether the weighing is a real balance or a figure for complete justice, sound judgment, and exact reckoning.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r5.speaker: المعتزلة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r5.claim: The Muʿtazila, preceded in this view by Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Aʿmash, deny a literal balance and take heaviness and lightness as abundance or scarcity of good deeds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r6.speaker: جمهور الأمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r6.claim: The majority affirm a real balance with a shaft, two pans, and a tongue, shown to all creatures to establish proof, justice, and the end of excuses.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r7.claim: The visible balance confirms the judgment alongside questioning, people’s admissions, testimony by limbs, prophets, angels, and witnesses.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r8.claim: Reports say the weighed objects are the records on which deeds were written; God creates heaviness or lightness in them, while reports about the balance’s dimensions and form have unsound chains.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r9.speaker: جمهور الأمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r9.claim: The majority explain plural balances by the multiplicity of objects weighed, although there is one balance.

SAMIN-DURR:7:9/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:9/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:7:9/r1.claim: بما كانوا modifies خسروا, with ما as a verbal noun; بآياتنا modifies يظلمون and is fronted for the verse ending.

SAMIN-DURR:7:9/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:9/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:7:9/r2.claim: The ba in يظلمون reflects an implied meaning of denial or rejection, comparable to آل عمران 3:11 and النمل 27:14.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r1.claim: One view weighs deeds themselves, which God turns into bodies; al-Baghawi reports this from Ibn Abbas, with traditions portraying Qur’an, surahs, and righteous deeds as visible forms.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r2.claim: A second view weighs the record of deeds; the report of the card bearing There is no god but God outweighing ninety-nine scrolls is graded sound by al-Tirmidhi.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r3.claim: A third view weighs the person: a very heavy man may weigh less than a gnat’s wing, while Ibn Masud’s thin legs outweigh Mount Uhud.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r4.claim: Ibn Kathir sees no conflict: deeds, their records or forms, and the people who performed them may all be weighed at different times.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389/r1.claim: The scales on Judgment Day weigh deeds with perfect justice; God wrongs no one, and the heavier scale brings success while the lighter one brings ruin.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r10.claim: Those whose scales are light lose their own selves, their chief capital, through persistently putting God's signs in the wrong place.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r9.speaker: الحسن
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r9.claim: Al-Hasan says the scale holding good deeds should naturally grow heavy, while the scale holding sins should grow light.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r1.claim: In a dialogue, the Prophet defines faith as belief in God, angels, books, messengers, Paradise and Hell, the balance, resurrection, and divine decree.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r10.claim: The balance has a tongue and two pans; heavy scales bring success, while light scales mean losing oneself and one's home in Paradise for wronging God's signs.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r2.claim: The weighing is justice; heavy scales mean good deeds, and the transmitted gloss for light scales also says good deeds.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن العيزار
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r3.claim: A caller beside the balance announces each person's lasting felicity or misery according to whether the scales are heavy or light.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r5.speaker: وهب بن منبه
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r5.claim: Only the endings of deeds are weighed: God grants a good ending to the one He wills good for and an evil ending to the one He wills evil for.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r6.speaker: الحارث الأعور
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r6.claim: Truth feels heavy to people of truth as it is heavy on the balance, and light to people of falsehood as it is light there.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r9.speaker: حذيفة
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r9.claim: Gabriel oversees the balances: an oppressor's good deeds are transferred to the victim, or the victim's sins to the oppressor if the oppressor has no good deeds.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r1.claim: Asked whether people remember their families at resurrection, the Prophet says not at the balance, when records fly, or at the bridge.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r2.claim: One more good deed than bad leads to Paradise and one more bad than good to Hell; equal deeds place a person among the people of the Heights, and a single grain can tip the balance.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r3.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r3.claim: A person whose outward state outweighs the inward has a light balance; one whose inward outweighs the outward has a heavy balance.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r4.speaker: جابر
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r4.claim: The Prophet says good and bad deeds are weighed; whichever side prevails determines entry to Paradise or Hell.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r5.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r5.claim: An angel announces a person's lasting felicity or misery according to whether the balance tips heavy or light.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r6.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r6.claim: The Prophet says people do not remember one another while the balance is placed, until each knows whether it is heavy or light.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r7.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r7.claim: The Prophet adds that people do not remember one another as records scatter until they know where each book lands, citing 69:19.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r8.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r8.claim: At the bridge over Hell, hooks and thorns detain whom God wills until they know whether they will escape.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r10.speaker: داود
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r10.claim: Dāwūd asks to see the Judgment scale and faints at its vast size; God says one date of charity can fill it if He is pleased with the servant.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r2.claim: Light scales reflect sins; those who lose themselves have damaged their sound original nature and earned punishment through their deeds.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r3.speaker: الحدادي
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r3.claim: Al-Ḥaddādī defines loss as losing one's capital; a person's capital is the self, so destroying it through bad deeds is self-loss.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r4.claim: Wronging God's signs means placing denial where belief should be; grammatically, ‘what’ is a verbal noun and ‘by Our signs’ modifies ‘wronging’ with denial implied.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r5.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r5.claim: The Najmī taʾwīl says the scale weighs people of truth and good deeds, not falsehood and its adherents; it cites the promise that no weight will be set for them.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r6.claim: A report describes a huge, tall, gluttonous man who weighs less than a mosquito's wing, supporting the view that people themselves may be weighed.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r7.claim: Some scholars say people are weighed, but the majority say deed records are weighed on a two-pan scale before witnesses to demonstrate justice and remove excuses.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r8.claim: A report has ninety-nine long scrolls weighed against a small card with the two testimonies; the scrolls fly up while the card weighs more.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r9.claim: A card was a small tag sewn into a garment to record its price.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r1.claim: Those whose balances are light lose themselves by wasting the innate disposition for Islam that every newborn possesses, or the disposition toward goodness at the root of human nature.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r2.claim: The causal phrase attaches to 'lost'; the prepositional phrase is advanced for the rhyme, ظلم is construed with ب for its sense of denial, and past plus present verbs indicate continued wrongdoing.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r3.speaker: بعض
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r3.claim: Some say unbelievers too have deeds weighed if those deeds do not depend on Islam; al-Qurtubi calls this correct and says it can lessen their punishment, as with Abu Talib.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r4.speaker: الكثير
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r4.claim: Many hold weighing is for Muslims only, since unbelievers' works are nullified and cannot lessen their punishment; al-Sakhawi says any mitigation for Abu Talib is a special exception.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p85/r5.claim: The passage does not address those whose good and bad deeds balance, identified by one opinion as the people of the Heights; some infer such a group does not exist, while a reply places them among those whose deeds are mixed and notes God's asa promises fulfillment.

ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r10.claim: Those with light scales have ruined themselves because they persistently deny God's signs and refuse to give them their due.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r5.claim: The conditional clauses explain the weighing's outcome: success follows heavy measures and loss follows light ones.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r7.claim: Lightness is a matching metaphor for the absence of good deeds, reinforced by the balance imagery and the explanation that they wronged God's signs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r5.claim: Loss is the opposite of profit; losing themselves means losing their own capacities for benefit, like a merchant who wastes all his capital and is ruined by it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r6.claim: The causal باء and مصدرية ما link their loss to persistent wrongdoing against the signs; the imperfect evokes repeated past denial, and ظَلَموا includes denying evidence.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r1.claim: Their denial is injustice because it suppresses evidence whose truth has been established and refuses to act on it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r2.claim: Fronting بآياتنا gives the signs emphasis.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r3.claim: The passage addresses believers who all did good and polytheists devoid of good; mixed believers are outside its purpose and discussed elsewhere.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r1.claim: He concludes that deeds are weighed by truth: those containing the truth required in worship succeed, while works lacking it leave their owners ruined for denying God’s signs.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r2.claim: Judgment applies each deed to the truth proper to it; reward follows in proportion to that truth, and failure to contain it leads to ruin, so the verses can be read literally.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r3.claim: Another interpretation takes weighing as justice and heavy scales as predominance of good deeds, treating the language as metaphor.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r4.claim: He rejects accounts that make the scales arbitrary and says each person has measures corresponding to the different truths in their deeds; the afterlife belongs wholly to truth and God.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r6.speaker: جابر
TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r6.claim: A report says good and evil deeds are weighed, and whichever side prevails determines entry into Paradise or Hell; the author accepts its content but not as an explanation of these verses.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r7.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r7.claim: Ali says a person whose outward appearance outweighs their inner state has a light scale, while inner reality outweighing outward appearance makes it heavy; the author says it does not explain the verses.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r1.speaker: عائشة
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r1.claim: A report says God fashioned the balance’s pans like heaven and earth and the path like a sword, saying he weighs and grants passage to whomever he wills.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r2.speaker: سلمان
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r2.claim: Al-Hakim reports a similar account from Salman.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r3.claim: He says these narrations depict an afterlife balance resembling the worldly instrument and are intended to make the idea accessible to unsophisticated hearers, as later reports clarify.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r4.speaker: هشام بن الحكم
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r4.claim: In a debate with a skeptic, Imam al-Sadiq says deeds are attributes rather than bodies, God does not need weighing to know their amount, and the balance means justice.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r1.claim: He explains deeds as moral qualities attached to actions, not the physical movements themselves: the same movement is lawful marriage or adultery according to its social or religious status.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r2.claim: The Imam’s argument has two parts: deeds as attributes have no physical weight, and God needs no weighing because nothing is hidden from him.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r3.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r3.claim: Some argue that embodied deeds can acquire weight, with the scale frightening sinners, encouraging the obedient, and displaying justice; they find problems in the Imam’s report.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r4.claim: He replies that deeds may appear embodied and justice may take the form of a balance; the report denies only worldly physical weight and does not require two-pan comparison.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r5.speaker: أمير المؤمنين عليه السلام
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r5.claim: A report says good deeds weigh down the balance while sins make it light; the author says this supports the truth in a deed as its measure.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r6.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r6.claim: Asked about the just balances, Imam al-Sadiq identifies them as the prophets and their successors.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r7.claim: He explains the report by saying prophets and Imams embody the measure of right action and belief.

TABATABAI:7:1-9/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r1.claim: The Quran’s ‘just balances’ means God’s just placement, not that the balance itself is justice; the wording ‘no soul is wronged’ shows that the justice belongs to God.

TABATABAI:7:1-9/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r2.claim: Commentators who take weighing as justice explain heaviness metaphorically as predominance of good deeds, and lightness as predominance of sins and loss of the self.

TABATABAI:7:1-9/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r3.claim: That interpretation must still identify a just criterion for mixed, unequal good and bad deeds; otherwise the outcome would be arbitrary and would not complete the proof against people.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r1.claim: He reads the weight as truth contained in deeds: good works have weight to the extent they embody truth, while evil is falsehood and has none.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r2.claim: The placed book identifies the truth in each deed and the weighing makes its amount manifest; he links this to judgment by truth and the book that speaks truth.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r3.claim: The plural ‘balances’ suits the distinct standards for different acts, since the truth of prayer differs from that of almsgiving, fasting, and pilgrimage.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r5.claim: If ‘balances’ means weighed deeds, as some commentators suggest, their account still leaves unclear what determines relative heaviness when good and bad acts are mixed.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r1.speaker: علي بن الحسين عليه السلام
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r1.claim: Ali ibn al-Husayn says scales and records are set up for Muslims; polytheists are driven to Hell in groups, and he cites the verse about no weight for disbelievers.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r2.claim: He notes that the narration alludes to the statement that God will not assign the disbelievers any weight on Judgment Day.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r4.claim: A report interprets ‘wronging Our signs’ as denying the Imams; the author treats this as one concrete instance of the broader meaning.

TABATABAI:7:8-9/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r1.claim: The verses portray good deeds as heavy and evil deeds as making the scales light, rather than weighing two piles and comparing their total mass.

TABATABAI:7:8-9/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r2.claim: Quranic parallels consistently place heaviness with good and lightness with evil, as in 23:102–103 and 101:6–10.

TABATABAI:7:8-9/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r3.claim: He proposes that each deed is tested by its own measure of truth: complete prayer, rightful almsgiving, and truthful speech exemplify standards that good deeds meet and sins fail.

TABATABAI:7:8-9/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r4.claim: The comparison with a physical balance illustrates a single measure placed against the item; the measure itself determines whether the item has matching weight or is rejected.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r1.claim: Judgment aims to reward or punish justly according to the quantity and quality of deeds, which requires a measure; here ‘weight’ names that measure.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r3.claim: Good deeds may receive more than their equivalent, bad deeds equivalent punishment, while repentance, intercession, or sheer divine mercy may forgive sins or increase rewards without violating justice.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r5.speaker: some commentators
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r5.claim: Some commentators say the things weighed are deeds made into tangible objects; others say they are the records of deeds.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r6.claim: Commentators differ over whether the weighing is a literal balance or metaphor; the manner and instrument are known to God.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r7.claim: For people, the essential point is that God records intentions, thoughts, feelings, words, and actions, then counts and judges them completely fairly, rewarding or punishing by their nature and amount.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r1.claim: The weighing refers to each person's deeds being weighed and judgment rendered on the Last Day.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r10.claim: Together these themes suggest a universal cosmic balance that grounds equitable transactions and measures human acts for recompense in the next life.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r11.claim: Like the questioning in 7:6, weighing does not mean God needs an external source of information or judgment to know how people should be judged.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r12.speaker: Z
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r12.claim: The weighing rebukes wrongdoers by making them acknowledge their wrongdoing and abandon excuses.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r13.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r13.claim: The balance assures people that they have not been wronged because all deeds are judged by the same scale.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r4.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r4.claim: A light balance belongs to those whose evil deeds outweigh their good deeds.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r7.claim: The balance image is a metaphor for Divine Judgment and appears in other Qur’anic passages.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r8.claim: The judgment image accords with Qur’anic commands to weigh fairly and honestly in commercial dealings.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r9.claim: The balance also fits the Qur’anic theme that creation is in due balance and that God sets the balance for the created order.

STUDYQURAN:7:intro/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:intro/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:intro/r8.claim: Verses 1–10 remind listeners to follow divine guidance and warn generally of the consequences of failing to do so.
